ev.ane_fc_bad_day.spell.ok: The lector priest wrote out a spell on a strip of papyrus, calling on Horus, son of Isis, rolled it up and slipped it into a little case on a cord. Every evening your mother kisses it before putting you to bed.
ev.ane_fc_bad_day.river: Keep the child away from the river
ev.ane_fc_bad_day.river.ok: The household decided: not one step towards the water. No bathing with the children, no washing with the women, no fishing with the men — let the crocodile wait in vain.
ev.ane_fc_bad_day.ignore.ok: "Let scribes count grain — fate is known to the gods," one of the elders snapped. The scroll was rolled up and never mentioned again.
ev.ane_fc_bad_day.title: An unlucky day
ev.ane_fc_bad_day.text: The temple scribe consulted the scroll of lucky and unlucky days — and his face darkened. Of the day you were born it says: "One born on this day will die by a crocodile." Your mother is in tears. A lector priest could write a spell against crocodiles and hang it round your neck in a little case — or you could simply be kept away from the river.
ev.ane_fc_bad_day.note: Calendars of lucky and unlucky days, such as the Cairo Calendar of the Ramesside period, went through every day of the year and sometimes foretold the fate of those born on it: "will die by a crocodile", "will die by a snake", "will die in honoured old age". People protected themselves with spells: the Magical Papyrus Harris of the same period contains charms against crocodiles, and written spells were worn round the neck in little cases.
ev.ane_fc_bad_day_croc.title: Crocodile at the landing
ev.ane_fc_bad_day_croc.text: You were drawing water at the landing when a crocodile lunged out of the mud. You leapt back, its jaws snapped right beside your leg, and, gasping, you felt for the spell-case at your throat. When your mother heard, she ran to the temple with an offering for Horus, and for a week you jumped at every splash.
ev.ane_fc_bad_day_swim.title: Can't swim
ev.ane_fc_bad_day_swim.text: All the children around swim like fish, but you were never allowed near the river. During the flood your boat capsized and you sank like a stone — one of the neighbours' youngsters dragged you out by the hair. Now the two of you are best friends, and at last you are learning to swim, though no one at home knows.
ev.ane_fc_lamashtu.ashipu.ok: The ashipu recited incantations until midnight, then carried the clay Lamashtu out beyond the city gate — with a comb, a spindle and tiny sandals. Towards morning you fell asleep and slept till noon.
ev.ane_fc_lamashtu.plaque.ok: Above the cradle they hung a clay plaque with a relief and an incantation: "I adjure you by Anu, your father…" Your mother touches it every time she passes.
ev.ane_fc_lamashtu.god.ok: Your father stood all night before the niche with the figure of the family's personal god, begging him to plead with the great gods. By morning you were quiet.
ev.ane_fc_lamashtu.title: Lamashtu at the door
ev.ane_fc_lamashtu.text: For the third night you have screamed and refused the breast, your mother cannot close her eyes, and the old women whisper: it is Lamashtu, daughter of Anu, prowling the rooftops in search of babies. An exorcist, an ashipu, could be called — he will model a figure of the demoness, give her a comb, a spindle and sandals for the road and send her away, but that costs dear. Or a clay plaque with an incantation can be hung by the cradle — or the family can pray to its personal god.
ev.ane_fc_lamashtu.note: Lamashtu was the most feared demoness of Mesopotamia, a killer of infants and women in childbirth. Incantations were written against her, amulets and plaques bearing her image were hung up, and an exorcist, the ashipu, "sent her away" provided with a comb, a spindle and sandals. Every family also had its own "personal god", an advocate before the great gods.
ev.ane_fc_lamashtu_ashipu.title: The exorcist's apprentice
ev.ane_fc_lamashtu_ashipu.text: The old ashipu who once sent Lamashtu away from your cradle recognised you in the street and called you to him. Now you carry his bag of herbs and clay, learning to model figures and recite incantations in which every word must be said at exactly the right moment.
ev.ane_fc_lamashtu_god.title: The personal god
ev.ane_fc_lamashtu_god.text: In a hard year you stood before the niche with the figure of the family's personal god — the one who, they say, pleaded for you when you were still in the cradle. You talked to him in a low voice for a long time, and in the morning your heart was light, as if someone large stood at your shoulder.
